title: Short Stuff: 1955 Le Mans Disaster
summary: Short Stuff episode on the 1955 Le Mans disaster at the Circuit de la Sarthe in France on June 11, 1955. Chuck and Josh explain the 24-hour endurance race format and the length of the track, then describe the pit-lane layout and the chain of events: Mike Hawthorne's Jaguar cut in front of Lance Macklin's Austin-Healey, Macklin swerved, Pierre Levegh's Mercedes was launched over the Austin-Healey, and it crashed into an embankment and a spectator stand and burst into flames, with car parts flying into the crowd. They cite roughly 83-84 spectator deaths, many injuries, and Levegh's death. They discuss the decision to let the race continue, Hawthorne winning, Hawthorne's death in a 1958 crash, Mercedes withdrawing and not racing again until the 1980s, official inquiries, and later safety changes including moving the pit road back from the track.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on the 1955 disaster at Le Mans and joke about a movie and Chuck's lack of interest in motorsports.

segments.title: The Le Mans race and track
segments.summary: Explanation of the 24-hour endurance format with three drivers per car, and the Circuit de la Sarthe, a roughly 8.5-mile track combining purpose-built racetrack and public roads. The distances covered in 24 hours are compared to long road trips.

segments.title: Speeds at Le Mans
segments.summary: Hosts note the track speed record of 253 mph set in 1988 and that cars in the 1950s reached roughly 120 to 150 mph.

segments.title: Pit lane design problem
segments.summary: Chuck describes the pit road, a quarter-mile stretch right along the edge of the track, with tightly packed cars and a need for sudden braking to enter the pits, which set the stage for the disaster.

segments.title: Tangent on NASCAR
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh briefly chat about NASCAR and a driver sponsored by UPS.

segments.title: Hawthorne's move and Macklin's swerve
segments.summary: Mike Hawthorne, driving a Jaguar, overtook Lance Macklin's Austin-Healey as Macklin was pulling aside for the pits, then braked hard. Macklin swerved left and into the path of Pierre Levegh's Mercedes.

segments.title: Levegh's crash and debris
segments.summary: Levegh's Mercedes was launched over the Austin-Healey, ran up an embankment, hit a concrete staircase and burst into flames. Car parts flew into the spectator area; Levegh died.

segments.title: Casualties
segments.summary: Debris cut through the grandstands at random. Chuck cites about 50 deaths at the scene and 83 spectator deaths, about 84 total, with close to 200 injured.

segments.title: Decision to continue the race
segments.summary: The race director allowed the 24-hour race to continue about two and a half hours in. Josh argues it helped emergency crews by avoiding a mass exodus of spectators; the hosts are unsure whether that was the reasoning.

segments.title: Aftermath for drivers and teams
segments.summary: Hawthorne won the race and celebrated, and never took responsibility. He died in a crash two years later while racing a friend. Mercedes withdrew at 1 a.m. and did not race again until the 1980s.

segments.title: Inquiries, outcry and track changes
segments.summary: Official inquiries absolved those involved and cited safety and layout problems. There was public outcry, more spectator barriers, and the pit road was moved about a quarter mile back from the track.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode and the show's production credit is read.
